pages.90:
READING PASSAGE 2

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14–26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.

Do literate women make better mothers?

Children in developing countries are healthier and more likely to survive past the age of five when their mothers can read and write. Experts in public health accepted this idea decades ago, but until now no one has been able to show that a woman's ability to read in itself improves her children's chances of survival.

Most literate women learnt to read in primary school, and the fact that a woman has had an education may simply indicate her family's wealth or that it values its children more highly. Now a long-term study carried out in Nicaragua has eliminated these factors by showing that teaching reading to poor adult women, who would otherwise have remained illiterate, has a direct effect on their children's health and survival.

In 1979, the government of Nicaragua established a number of social programmes, including a National Literacy Crusade. By 1985, about 300,000 illiterate adults from all over the country, many of whom had never attended primary school, had learnt how to read, write and use numbers.

During this period, researchers from the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine, the Central American Institute of Health in Nicaragua, the National Autonomous University of Nicaragua and the Costa Rican Institute of Health interviewed nearly 3,000 women, some of whom had learnt to read as children, some during the literacy crusade and some who had never learnt at all. The women were asked how many children they had given birth to and how many of them had died in infancy. The research teams also examined the surviving children to find out how well-nourished they were.

The investigators' findings were striking. In the late 1970s, the infant mortality rate for the children of illiterate mothers was around 110 deaths per thousand live births. At this point in their lives, those mothers who later went on to learn to read had a similar level of child mortality (105/1000). For women educated in primary school, however, the infant mortality rate was significantly lower, at 80 per thousand.
pages.91:
In 1985, after the National Literacy Crusade had ended, the infant mortality figures for those who remained illiterate and for those educated in primary school remained more or less unchanged. For those women who learnt to read through the campaign, the infant mortality rate was 84 per thousand, an impressive 21 points lower than for those women who were still illiterate. The children of the newly-literate mothers were also better nourished than those of women who could not read.

Why are the children of literate mothers better off? According to Peter Sandiford of the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine, no one knows for certain. Child health was not on the curriculum during the women's lessons, so he and his colleagues are looking at other factors. They are working with the same group of 3,000 women, to try to find out whether reading mothers make better use of hospitals and clinics, opt for smaller families, exert more control at home, learn modern childcare techniques more quickly, or whether they merely have more respect for themselves and their children.

The Nicaraguan study may have important implications for governments and aid agencies that need to know where to direct their resources. Sandiford says that there is increasing evidence that female education, at any age, is 'an important health intervention in its own right'. The results of the study lend support to the World Bank's recommendation that education budgets in developing countries should be increased, not just to help their economies, but also to improve child health.

'We've known for a long time that maternal education is important,' says John Cleland of the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine. 'But we thought that even if we started educating girls today, we'd have to wait a generation for the pay-off. The Nicaraguan study suggests we may be able to bypass that.'

Cleland warns that the Nicaraguan crusade was special in many ways, and similar campaigns elsewhere might not work as well. It is notoriously difficult to teach adults skills that do not have an immediate impact on their everyday lives, and many literacy campaigns in other countries have been much less successful. 'The crusade was part of a larger effort to bring a better life to the people,' says Cleland. Replicating these conditions in other countries will be a major challenge for development workers.

evidence.text: By 1985, about 300,000 illiterate adults from all over the country ... had learnt how to read, write and use numbers.

14.reason: The crusade taught illiterate adults nationally; option B is the only list item that denotes the adult male and female population without adding children.

distractors.A: Child literacy is a type of literacy, not a group of illiterate people taught by the crusade.
distractors.C: The international research team investigated the effects; it was not the population taught.
distractors.D: Medical care is neither a group of people nor the object population of the crusade.
distractors.E: Mortality is an outcome measure, not a group of learners.
distractors.F: Maternal literacy is the explanatory factor studied, not the full population taught by the national campaign.
distractors.G: The passage says illiterate adults; it does not say the crusade taught children.
distractors.H: Paternal literacy is a type of literacy, not a group of learners.
distractors.I: A National Literacy Crusade is the programme itself, not the people it taught.
distractors.J: Family wealth is a possible confounding factor, not a group of learners.

evidence.text: Children in developing countries are healthier and more likely to survive past the age of five when their mothers can read and write.

15.reason: The known connection is between child health and mothers' ability to read and write, i.e. maternal literacy.

distractors.A: The passage discusses mothers' literacy, not children's literacy.
distractors.B: Men and women names a population and does not complete the causal connection.
distractors.C: The research team investigated the question; it is not the factor connected with child health.
distractors.D: Medical care is explored as one possible mechanism, not the long-known correlation stated here.
distractors.E: Mortality is one measure of child health, not the maternal factor connected with it.
distractors.G: Adults and children names people, not the relevant literacy variable.
distractors.H: The passage gives no connection between paternal literacy and child health.
distractors.I: The crusade supplied the natural experiment; it is not the long-known health factor.
distractors.J: Family wealth is a confounder that the study sought to eliminate, not the target connection.

evidence.text: researchers from the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine, the Central American Institute of Health in Nicaragua, the National Autonomous University of Nicaragua and the Costa Rican Institute of Health interviewed nearly 3,000 women

16.reason: Researchers from institutions in Britain, Nicaragua and Costa Rica jointly investigated the question, so they form an international research team.

distractors.A: Child literacy is a topic, not an investigating agent.
distractors.B: Men and women were participants in the literacy campaign, not the named investigators.
distractors.D: Medical care is a possible explanatory mechanism, not an investigator.
distractors.E: Mortality is measured by the study and cannot perform an investigation.
distractors.F: Maternal literacy is the variable being investigated, not the agent.
distractors.G: Adults and children are population groups, not the named investigators.
distractors.H: Paternal literacy is neither the investigator nor a focus of this study.
distractors.I: The National Literacy Crusade created the study conditions but did not itself conduct the research described.
distractors.J: Family wealth is a factor controlled for, not an investigating body.

evidence.text: the fact that a woman has had an education may simply indicate her family's wealth or that it values its children more highly. Now a long-term study carried out in Nicaragua has eliminated these factors

17.reason: The summary pairs the blank with 'attitudes to children'; the original names the two confounders as family wealth and how highly the family values its children.

distractors.A: Child literacy is not one of the confounders named and eliminated.
distractors.B: Men and women are people taught, not an eliminated explanatory factor.
distractors.C: The research team performs the investigation; it is not eliminated from it.
distractors.D: Medical care is considered later as a possible mechanism and is not the factor paired with attitudes here.
distractors.E: Mortality is the measured outcome, not a confounder eliminated by the study design.
distractors.F: Maternal literacy is the variable whose independent effect the study is trying to establish, not eliminate.
distractors.G: Adults and children are participant groups, not a confounding factor.
distractors.H: Paternal literacy is not mentioned as an eliminated factor.
distractors.I: The crusade enables comparison and is not eliminated.

evidence.text: teaching reading to poor adult women, who would otherwise have remained illiterate, has a direct effect on their children's health and survival

18.reason: After confounders are removed, the study shows that mothers' literacy itself can improve infant health and survival.

distractors.A: The study did not test whether children's own literacy improves infant survival.
distractors.B: Men and women is a population description and cannot denote the causal factor.
distractors.C: A research team can demonstrate an effect but is not the factor that improves infant health.
distractors.D: Medical care is only one possible pathway being investigated and is not the demonstrated intervention in this sentence.
distractors.E: Mortality is an outcome and does not improve health or survival.
distractors.G: Adults and children is a population description, not the causal variable.
distractors.H: Paternal literacy is not studied or shown to have this effect.
distractors.I: The crusade was the delivery mechanism; the conclusion isolates literacy acquired by mothers rather than the campaign label itself.
distractors.J: Family wealth was eliminated as a confounder rather than shown to be the independent intervention.

evidence.text: interviewed nearly 3,000 women, some of whom had learnt to read as children, some during the literacy crusade and some who had never learnt at all

19.reason: The total sample and three categories are given, but the number in the childhood-literacy category is not stated.

distractors.YES: 'Some' does not establish that the subgroup numbered about one thousand.
distractors.NO: The passage does not give a different number for that subgroup, so the claim is not contradicted either.

evidence.text: the infant mortality rate for the children of illiterate mothers was around 110 deaths per thousand live births ... For women educated in primary school, however, the infant mortality rate was significantly lower, at 80 per thousand.

20.reason: The passage explicitly contrasts about 110 per thousand with a significantly lower 80 per thousand, so the levels were not approximately the same.

distractors.YES: The figures and the word 'significantly' directly oppose the statement.
distractors.NOT GIVEN: Both comparison figures are explicitly supplied.

evidence.text: the infant mortality rate for the children of illiterate mothers was around 110 deaths per thousand live births ... [in 1985] the infant mortality figures for those who remained illiterate ... remained more or less unchanged

21.reason: The pre-crusade rate was about 110 and the later figure for women who stayed illiterate was described as more or less unchanged.

distractors.NO: No later rise or fall for the still-illiterate group is reported; the passage says unchanged.
distractors.NOT GIVEN: The before figure and the after-change description are both stated.

evidence.text: those mothers who later went on to learn to read had ... child mortality (105/1000) ... [later] 84 per thousand, an impressive 21 points lower ... [the other groups] remained more or less unchanged

22.reason: The campaign group fell by 21 points while the illiterate and primary-school groups remained broadly unchanged, making this the greatest change.

distractors.NO: The comparison across all three groups confirms rather than contradicts the greatest change.
distractors.NOT GIVEN: The before and after figures and the unchanged comparison groups are supplied.

evidence.text: For women educated in primary school ... 80 per thousand ... For those women who learnt to read through the campaign, the infant mortality rate was 84 per thousand

23.reason: The campaign group's 84 per thousand was higher, not lower, than the primary-school group's unchanged rate of about 80.

distractors.YES: A large improvement does not make 84 the lowest rate when another group is at 80.
distractors.NOT GIVEN: The necessary rates for both groups are explicitly available.

evidence.text: The children of the newly-literate mothers were also better nourished than those of women who could not read.

24.reason: The passage gives only a relative comparison. It does not classify the illiterate mothers' children as severely malnourished.

distractors.YES: 'Less well nourished' than another group does not entail 'severely malnourished'.
distractors.NO: The passage does not state that these children were not severely malnourished; it simply omits the severity classification.

25.answerText: The effects of maternal literacy programmes can be seen very quickly.

evidence.text: we'd have to wait a generation for the pay-off. The Nicaraguan study suggests we may be able to bypass that.

25.reason: The study suggests the health benefit need not wait for the next generation, so programme effects may appear quickly.

distractors.A: The passage does not say educating mature women is better than educating girls; it says adult education may produce benefits sooner than previously expected.
distractors.B: Cleland explicitly warns that similar campaigns elsewhere might not work as well.
distractors.D: The passage recommends education for both economic and child-health benefits, but does not say improved child health quickly changes the economy.

26.answerText: Money spent on female education will improve child health.

evidence.text: The results of the study lend support to the World Bank's recommendation that education budgets in developing countries should be increased, not just to help their economies, but also to improve child health.

26.reason: The stated policy implication is that increased education spending, specifically female education in context, can improve child health.

distractors.A: No superiority claim is made between adult women and young girls.
distractors.B: The final paragraph warns that the special Nicaraguan conditions may not be replicable elsewhere.
distractors.D: The causal direction and speed claimed in D are absent; the text says education spending can improve both economies and child health.
